items.stem: What is meant by absolute advantage?
options: The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country
The ability of a country to produce more of a good than another country with the same resources
Having a larger population than a trading partner
Exporting more than a country imports
items.answer: The ability of a country to produce more of a good than another country with the same resources
items.markingKey: Absolute advantage: higher output per unit of resource (or the same output with fewer resources).

items.stem: Explain the difference between absolute advantage and comparative advantage.
items.answer: Absolute advantage means producing more of a good than another country with the same resources. Comparative advantage means producing a good at a lower opportunity cost, i.e. giving up less of the other good.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: absolute = more output from same resources; 1 mark: comparative = lower opportunity cost [2]

items.stem: Explain why a country with an absolute advantage in both goods can still benefit from trade.
items.answer: Its opportunity costs will still differ from the other country’s; if it specialises where its advantage is greatest (lowest opportunity cost) and trades, both countries can consume beyond their own PPCs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: opportunity costs differ; 1 mark: specialise in lower-OC good; 1 mark: consume beyond PPC/both gain [3]

items.stem: One worker in Marvona can produce either 5 tonnes of wheat or 8 cars a week. One worker in Gorvania can produce either 8 tonnes of wheat or 6 cars a week. On the basis of comparative advantage, which pattern of specialisation would increase total output?
options: Marvona should specialise in wheat and Gorvania in cars
Each country should produce both goods equally
Gorvania should specialise in wheat and Marvona in cars
Neither country can gain from specialisation
items.answer: Gorvania should specialise in wheat and Marvona in cars
items.markingKey: OC of 1 unit of wheat: Marvona 1.6, Gorvania 0.75 cars; Gorvania has the lower OC of wheat.

items.stem: One worker in Westaria can produce either 12 tonnes of maize or 5 computers a week. One worker in Gorvania can produce either 8 tonnes of maize or 2 computers a week. (a) Calculate the opportunity cost of each good in each country. (b) State which country has a comparative advantage in each good.
items.answer: (a) OC of 1 unit of maize: Westaria = 5/12 = 0.42 computers; Gorvania = 2/8 = 0.25 computers. OC of 1 unit of computers: Westaria = 2.4 tonnes of maize; Gorvania = 4 tonnes of maize. (b) Gorvania has a comparative advantage in maize and Westaria in computers.
items.markingKey: (a) four opportunity costs, 2 marks for all correct, 1 for two [2] (b) both comparative advantages [1] [3]

items.stem: One worker in Nordavia can produce either 8 tonnes of maize or 4 computers a week. One worker in Marvona can produce either 4 tonnes of maize or 6 computers a week. (a) Identify which country has an absolute advantage in each good. (b) Using opportunity costs, explain which good each country should specialise in. (c) State the range of terms of trade (units of computers per unit of maize) within which both countries gain.
items.answer: (a) Nordavia has an absolute advantage in maize and Marvona in computers. (b) OC of 1 unit of maize: Nordavia = 4/8 = 0.5 computers; Marvona = 6/4 = 1.5 computers. OC of 1 unit of computers: Nordavia = 2 tonnes of maize; Marvona = 0.67 tonnes of maize. Nordavia has a comparative advantage in maize and Marvona in computers. (c) 1 unit of maize must exchange for between 0.5 and 1.5 computers; e.g. 1 unit of maize = 1 computers benefits both.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) opportunity costs [1]; specialisation [1] (c) range [2] [5]

items.stem: Extract: Fendaria and Ostrelia are negotiating a free trade agreement. One worker in Fendaria can produce 6 tonnes of wheat or 12 cars a week; one worker in Ostrelia can produce 10 tonnes of wheat or 2 cars. Over the last five years Fendaria’s export price index has moved to 110 and its import price index to 94 (base year = 100). Trade unions in Fendaria fear job losses in its wheat industry, while business groups argue that tariff-free access to a larger market will bring economies of scale. Both countries are members of the WTO. (a) Calculate Fendaria’s terms of trade index and state whether it has improved since the base year. (b) Explain the difference between a free trade area and a customs union.
items.answer: (a) 110/94 × 100 = 117; improved (favourable). (b) An FTA removes internal tariffs only; a customs union also has a common external tariff.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: 110/94 × 100 = 117; improved (favourable). [2] (b) Credit: An FTA removes internal tariffs only; a customs union also has a common external tariff. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Nordavia and Zentara are negotiating a free trade agreement. One worker in Nordavia can produce 5 bales of cotton or 8 pairs of shoes a week; one worker in Zentara can produce 12 bales of cotton or 6 pairs of shoes. Over the last five years Nordavia’s export price index has moved to 110 and its import price index to 100 (base year = 100). Trade unions in Nordavia fear job losses in its cotton industry, while business groups argue that tariff-free access to a larger market will bring economies of scale. Both countries are members of the WTO. (a) Calculate Nordavia’s terms of trade index and state whether it has improved since the base year. (b) Explain why trade unions fear job losses.
items.answer: (a) 110/100 × 100 = 110; improved (favourable). (b) Resources move out of the industry with comparative disadvantage; cheaper imports replace domestic output; workers may be occupationally immobile.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: 110/100 × 100 = 110; improved (favourable). [2] (b) Credit: Resources move out of the industry with comparative disadvantage; cheaper imports replace domestic output; workers may be occupationally immobile. [3]

items.stem: What is meant by comparative advantage?
options: The ability of a country to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country
Having lower wages than a trading partner
A surplus on the current account
The ability to produce more of every good than another country
items.answer: The ability of a country to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country
items.markingKey: Comparative advantage depends on opportunity cost, not on absolute output.

items.stem: One worker in Ostrelia can produce either 10 bales of cotton or 10 pairs of shoes a week. One worker in Pelora can produce either 3 bales of cotton or 4 pairs of shoes a week. Which country has an absolute advantage in cotton?
options: Ostrelia
Pelora
Neither country
Both countries equally
items.answer: Ostrelia
items.markingKey: Absolute advantage: higher output per worker (10 vs 3 bales of cotton).

items.stem: Extract: Dravonia and Merania are negotiating a free trade agreement. One worker in Dravonia can produce 4 tonnes of wheat or 6 cars a week; one worker in Merania can produce 3 tonnes of wheat or 12 cars. Over the last five years Dravonia’s export price index has moved to 105 and its import price index to 94 (base year = 100). Trade unions in Dravonia fear job losses in its cars industry, while business groups argue that tariff-free access to a larger market will bring economies of scale. Both countries are members of the WTO. (a) Calculate Dravonia’s terms of trade index and state whether it has improved since the base year. (b) Explain the difference between a free trade area and a customs union.
items.answer: (a) 105/94 × 100 = 111.7; improved (favourable). (b) An FTA removes internal tariffs only; a customs union also has a common external tariff.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: 105/94 × 100 = 111.7; improved (favourable). [2] (b) Credit: An FTA removes internal tariffs only; a customs union also has a common external tariff. [2]

items.stem: What is meant by free trade?
options: Trade that takes place without money
International trade without government restrictions such as tariffs or quotas
Trade only between members of a trading bloc
Trade where exports equal imports
items.answer: International trade without government restrictions such as tariffs or quotas
items.markingKey: No barriers imposed by governments.

items.stem: Explain how specialisation according to comparative advantage increases world output.
items.answer: Each country moves resources into the good it produces at lowest opportunity cost, so the same resources produce more in total; trade then lets countries share the extra output.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: resources moved to lowest-OC use; 1 mark: total output rises; 1 mark: trade distributes the gains [3]

items.stem: Explain two benefits of free trade for a developing economy.
items.answer: Access to larger markets for exports, raising income and employment; access to cheaper capital goods and technology; competition and FDI raise efficiency.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for two benefits, 1 mark each for explanation [4]

items.stem: Selmaria and Quentara each have 100 workers. One worker in Selmaria can produce 6 bales of cotton or 10 pairs of shoes; one worker in Quentara can produce 12 bales of cotton or 4 pairs of shoes. Before trade, each country uses half its workers in each industry. What is the combined output of the two countries before trade?
options: 1200 bales of cotton and 1000 pairs of shoes
450 bales of cotton and 350 pairs of shoes
900 bales of cotton and 700 pairs of shoes
1800 bales of cotton and 1400 pairs of shoes
items.answer: 900 bales of cotton and 700 pairs of shoes
items.markingKey: 50 × (6 + 12) = 900 bales of cotton; 50 × (10 + 4) = 700 pairs of shoes.

items.stem: Zentara and Nordavia each have 100 workers. One worker in Zentara can produce 4 bales of cotton or 8 pairs of shoes; one worker in Nordavia can produce 2 bales of cotton or 3 pairs of shoes. Before trade, each country uses half its workers in each industry. (a) Calculate the combined output before trade. (b) Calculate the combined output if Nordavia specialises completely in cotton and Zentara in shoes. (c) Comment on the change.
items.answer: (a)/(b) Before: 300 bales of cotton and 550 pairs of shoes. After complete specialisation (Nordavia in cotton, Zentara in shoes): 200 bales of cotton and 800 pairs of shoes. (c) Change: −100 bales of cotton, +250 pairs of shoes. Output of cotton falls, so complete specialisation does not raise output of both goods; partial specialisation would be needed for that, but valued at any terms of trade between the two opportunity-cost ratios, total output is still higher than before.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) [1] (c) comment on change [1] [3]

items.stem: Extract: Fendaria and Sundara are negotiating a free trade agreement. One worker in Fendaria can produce 10 tonnes of rice or 6 metres of cloth a week; one worker in Sundara can produce 5 tonnes of rice or 8 metres of cloth. Over the last five years Fendaria’s export price index has moved to 110 and its import price index to 112 (base year = 100). Trade unions in Fendaria fear job losses in its cloth industry, while business groups argue that tariff-free access to a larger market will bring economies of scale. Both countries are members of the WTO. (a) Using opportunity costs, explain which country has a comparative advantage in rice. (b) Calculate Fendaria’s terms of trade index and state whether it has improved since the base year.
items.answer: (a) Fendaria, because it has the lower opportunity cost of rice (Fendaria: 0.6, Sundara: 1.6 metres of cloth per unit). (b) 110/112 × 100 = 98.2; worsened (unfavourable).
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Fendaria, because it has the lower opportunity cost of rice (Fendaria: 0.6, Sundara: 1.6 metres of cloth per unit). [2] (b) Credit: 110/112 × 100 = 98.2; worsened (unfavourable). [2]

items.stem: Explain why free trade may not benefit everyone in an economy.
items.answer: Workers and firms in industries that cannot compete with imports may lose jobs and income; resources are not perfectly mobile, so structural unemployment can result.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: losers in import-competing industries; 1 mark: factor immobility/structural unemployment [2]

items.stem: Esteria and Westaria each have 200 workers. One worker in Esteria can produce 12 kilograms of tea or 12 televisions; one worker in Westaria can produce 10 kilograms of tea or 3 televisions. Before trade, each country uses half its workers in each industry. (a) Explain which good each country should specialise in. (b) Calculate the combined output before trade and after complete specialisation. (c) Explain why both countries need to trade at a suitable rate of exchange to share the gains. (d) Discuss whether specialisation would benefit everyone in both countries.
items.answer: (a) OC of 1 unit of tea: Esteria 1, Westaria 0.3 televisions, so Westaria specialises in tea and Esteria in televisions. (b) Before: 2200 kilograms of tea and 1500 televisions. After complete specialisation (Westaria in tea, Esteria in televisions): 2000 kilograms of tea and 2400 televisions. Change: −200 kilograms of tea, +900 televisions. (c) Each country now produces only one good, so must trade; the terms of trade must lie between the opportunity-cost ratios (0.3–1 televisions per unit of tea) for both to gain. Output of tea falls, so complete specialisation does not raise output of both goods; partial specialisation would be needed for that, but valued at any terms of trade between the two opportunity-cost ratios, total output is still higher than before. (d) Workers in contracting industries face structural unemployment; transport costs and rising opportunity costs reduce gains; over-specialisation risk; consumers gain overall; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) before [1]; after [1] (c) terms of trade range [2] (d) winners and losers, judgement [3] [9]

items.stem: How is the terms of trade index calculated?
options: (Index of import prices ÷ index of export prices) × 100
(Value of exports ÷ value of imports) × 100
(Index of average export prices ÷ index of average import prices) × 100
Export volume minus import volume
items.answer: (Index of average export prices ÷ index of average import prices) × 100
items.markingKey: ToT = Px index / Pm index × 100.

items.stem: Explain two causes of an improvement in a country’s terms of trade.
items.answer: A rise in world demand for its exports raising their prices; an appreciation of its currency; higher domestic inflation than abroad; falling world prices of its imports (e.g. oil for an importer).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for two causes, 1 mark each for explanation [4]

items.stem: Explain why an improvement in the terms of trade is not necessarily good for an economy.
items.answer: If it results from higher export prices due to inflation or appreciation, export volumes may fall when demand is price elastic, worsening the current account and raising unemployment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: loss of price competitiveness; 1 mark: depends on PED/effect on export revenue and jobs [2]

items.stem: In Tarvia, with 2018 = 100, the export price index in 2023 was 112 and the import price index was 90. Calculate the terms of trade index for 2023.

In Rovania, with 2018 = 100, the export price index in 2023 was 88 and the import price index was 110. (a) Calculate the terms of trade index for 2023. (b) State whether the terms of trade have improved or worsened, and explain what this means.
items.answer: (a) 88/110 × 100 = 80. (b) They have worsened (unfavourable): a given quantity of exports now buys fewer imports than in 2018.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) direction [1]; meaning [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: Esteria and Umbria Nova are negotiating a free trade agreement. One worker in Esteria can produce 4 cubic metres of timber or 5 solar panels a week; one worker in Umbria Nova can produce 10 cubic metres of timber or 3 solar panels. Over the last five years Esteria’s export price index has moved to 105 and its import price index to 100 (base year = 100). Trade unions in Esteria fear job losses in its timber industry, while business groups argue that tariff-free access to a larger market will bring economies of scale. Both countries are members of the WTO. (a) Using opportunity costs, explain which country has a comparative advantage in timber. (b) Calculate Esteria’s terms of trade index and state whether it has improved since the base year.
items.answer: (a) Umbria Nova, because it has the lower opportunity cost of timber (Esteria: 1.25, Umbria Nova: 0.3 solar panels per unit). (b) 105/100 × 100 = 105; improved (favourable).
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Umbria Nova, because it has the lower opportunity cost of timber (Esteria: 1.25, Umbria Nova: 0.3 solar panels per unit). [2] (b) Credit: 105/100 × 100 = 105; improved (favourable). [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between the terms of trade and the balance of trade.
items.answer: The terms of trade is the ratio of export prices to import prices; the balance of trade is the value of exports of goods minus the value of imports of goods.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: ToT price ratio; 1 mark: balance of trade value difference [2]

items.stem: Extract: Quentara and Ostrelia are negotiating a free trade agreement. One worker in Quentara can produce 4 cubic metres of timber or 12 solar panels a week; one worker in Ostrelia can produce 5 cubic metres of timber or 2 solar panels. Over the last five years Quentara’s export price index has moved to 110 and its import price index to 100 (base year = 100). Trade unions in Quentara fear job losses in its timber industry, while business groups argue that tariff-free access to a larger market will bring economies of scale. Both countries are members of the WTO. (a) Calculate Quentara’s terms of trade index and state whether it has improved since the base year. (b) Explain why trade unions fear job losses.
items.answer: (a) 110/100 × 100 = 110; improved (favourable). (b) Resources move out of the industry with comparative disadvantage; cheaper imports replace domestic output; workers may be occupationally immobile.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: 110/100 × 100 = 110; improved (favourable). [2] (b) Credit: Resources move out of the industry with comparative disadvantage; cheaper imports replace domestic output; workers may be occupationally immobile. [3]

items.stem: What distinguishes a customs union from a free trade area?
options: A customs union has free movement of labour
A free trade area has a common external tariff
A customs union has a common external tariff
A customs union has a single currency
items.answer: A customs union has a common external tariff
items.markingKey: FTA members keep separate external tariffs.

items.stem: Explain the difference between trade creation and trade diversion.
items.answer: Trade creation: joining a bloc replaces high-cost domestic production with lower-cost imports from members (efficiency gain). Trade diversion: the common external tariff causes imports to switch from lower-cost non-members to higher-cost members (efficiency loss).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: trade creation explained; 1 mark: trade diversion explained; 1 mark: efficiency gain vs loss [3]

items.stem: Explain two benefits to a country of joining a customs union.
items.answer: Tariff-free access to a larger market (exports, economies of scale); greater competition raises efficiency; trade creation lowers prices; more FDI; greater bargaining power in trade negotiations.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for two benefits, 1 mark each for explanation [4]

items.stem: Members have free internal trade, a common external tariff and free movement of labour and capital. What type of trading bloc is described?
options: Free trade area
Common market
World Trade Organization
Customs union
items.answer: Common market
items.markingKey: Common market: customs union plus free movement of factors of production.

items.stem: Two countries agree that both will charge a 10% tariff on cars imported from outside their bloc, and none on cars traded between them. What type of trading bloc is described? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Customs union: common external tariff with internal free trade.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Customs union; 1 mark: explanation – common external tariff with internal free trade. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Halvoria and Selmaria are negotiating a free trade agreement. One worker in Halvoria can produce 6 tonnes of rice or 2 metres of cloth a week; one worker in Selmaria can produce 8 tonnes of rice or 12 metres of cloth. Over the last five years Halvoria’s export price index has moved to 92 and its import price index to 94 (base year = 100). Trade unions in Halvoria fear job losses in its cloth industry, while business groups argue that tariff-free access to a larger market will bring economies of scale. Both countries are members of the WTO. (a) Calculate the opportunity cost of 1 unit of rice in each country. (b) Explain the difference between a free trade area and a customs union.
items.answer: (a) Halvoria: 0.33 metres of cloth; Selmaria: 1.5 metres of cloth. (b) An FTA removes internal tariffs only; a customs union also has a common external tariff.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Halvoria: 0.33 metres of cloth; Selmaria: 1.5 metres of cloth. [2] (b) Credit: An FTA removes internal tariffs only; a customs union also has a common external tariff. [2]

items.stem: Explain why the WTO may find it difficult to achieve free trade.
items.answer: Decisions need consensus among many members with conflicting interests; governments face domestic pressure to protect industries; disputes over agriculture subsidies and developing-country exemptions.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: consensus/conflicting interests; 1 mark: domestic political pressure or example [2]

items.stem: Tarvia imports textiles. Before joining a customs union, Tarvia charged a 20% tariff on all imports. Gorvania (outside the union) supplies textiles at $60 per unit and Zentara (a union partner) at $63 per unit. After joining, imports from Zentara are tariff-free, while the common external tariff on Gorvania stays at 20%. After Tarvia joins, what is the price of textiles imported from Gorvania?
Which principle explains why a country with an absolute advantage in all goods can still gain from trade?
options: The principle of absolute advantage
The law of diminishing returns
The principle of comparative advantage
The law of demand
items.answer: The principle of comparative advantage
items.markingKey: Opportunity costs differ, so both countries gain by specialising according to comparative advantage.

items.stem: Explain how comparative advantage can be shown using production possibility curves.
items.answer: With constant costs each PPC is a straight line; its slope is the opportunity cost. If the slopes differ, each country has a comparative advantage in the good it gives up least of the other good to produce.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: slope = opportunity cost; 1 mark: different slopes = comparative advantage [2]

items.stem: Explain two limitations of the theory of comparative advantage.
items.answer: It assumes constant costs, no transport costs and perfect factor mobility; in reality costs rise with specialisation, transport costs and trade barriers reduce gains, and comparative advantage changes over time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each for two limitations, 1 mark each for explanation [4]

items.stem: Selmaria has a large supply of low-wage, low-skilled labour and exports garments. What is the most likely source of this country’s comparative advantage?
options: Comparative advantage based on natural resources
Comparative advantage based on labour abundance
Comparative advantage based on capital and technology
Comparative advantage based on human capital
items.answer: Comparative advantage based on labour abundance
items.markingKey: Comparative advantage based on labour abundance: labour-intensive goods have a low opportunity cost where labour is abundant.

items.stem: One worker in Korvia can produce either 5 tonnes of maize or 6 computers a week. One worker in Ostrelia can produce either 3 tonnes of maize or 5 computers a week. On the basis of comparative advantage, which pattern of specialisation would increase total output?
options: Ostrelia should specialise in maize and Korvia in computers
Neither country can gain from specialisation
Korvia should specialise in maize and Ostrelia in computers
Korvia should produce both goods
items.answer: Korvia should specialise in maize and Ostrelia in computers
items.markingKey: OC of 1 unit of maize: Korvia 1.2, Ostrelia 1.67 computers; Korvia has the lower OC of maize.

items.stem: Selmaria is a lower-middle-income economy that exports agricultural goods and imports most of its manufactured goods. Explain why a country may gain from specialising according to comparative advantage even if it has an absolute disadvantage in all goods.
items.answer: Opportunity costs differ; specialising in the good with the smaller disadvantage; trade at terms between OC ratios; consumption beyond PPC.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Opportunity costs differ; specialising in the good with the smaller disadvantage; trade at terms between OC ratios; consumption beyond PPC. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: Which is a benefit of free trade for consumers?
options: Lower prices and a wider choice of goods
Guaranteed employment in domestic industries
Fewer foreign firms in the market
Higher prices for imported goods
items.answer: Lower prices and a wider choice of goods
items.markingKey: Competition and access to lower-cost producers.

items.stem: Explain how free trade can benefit consumers.
items.answer: Imports from lower-cost producers lower prices, competition improves quality, and consumers gain a wider choice of products.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: lower prices; 1 mark: choice/quality [2]

items.stem: Juniper Brands expands output fourfold after gaining access to export markets, and its average cost falls. Which effect of free trade and specialisation does this illustrate?
options: Increased efficiency through competition
Benefit to consumers
Economies of scale
Risk of over-specialisation
items.answer: Economies of scale
items.markingKey: Economies of scale: a larger market allows lower long-run average cost.

items.stem: Gorvania earns 80% of its export revenue from cocoa and suffers when the world price halves. Which effect of free trade and specialisation does this illustrate? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Risk of over-specialisation: dependence on one export makes income volatile.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Risk of over-specialisation; 1 mark: explanation – dependence on one export makes income volatile. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Nordavia and Marvona are negotiating a free trade agreement. One worker in Nordavia can produce 10 bags of coffee or 10 machine tools a week; one worker in Marvona can produce 5 bags of coffee or 6 machine tools. Over the last five years Nordavia’s export price index has moved to 118 and its import price index to 112 (base year = 100). Trade unions in Nordavia fear job losses in its machine tools industry, while business groups argue that tariff-free access to a larger market will bring economies of scale. Both countries are members of the WTO. (a) Calculate Nordavia’s terms of trade index and state whether it has improved since the base year. (b) Explain why trade unions fear job losses.
items.answer: (a) 118/112 × 100 = 105.4; improved (favourable). (b) Resources move out of the industry with comparative disadvantage; cheaper imports replace domestic output; workers may be occupationally immobile.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: 118/112 × 100 = 105.4; improved (favourable). [2] (b) Credit: Resources move out of the industry with comparative disadvantage; cheaper imports replace domestic output; workers may be occupationally immobile. [3]

items.stem: What is meant by an improvement in the terms of trade?
options: Import prices rise relative to export prices
The current account moves into surplus
Each unit of exports buys more imports than before
The volume of exports rises
items.answer: Each unit of exports buys more imports than before
items.markingKey: Export prices rise relative to import prices.

items.stem: Explain how a rise in world demand for a country’s main export can improve its terms of trade and its current account at the same time.
items.answer: Higher demand raises the world price of the export (ToT improves) and also the quantity sold, so export revenue rises and the current account improves.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: price rises/ToT; 1 mark: revenue rises/current account improves [2]

items.stem: Over a year, the average price of Loristan’s exports rose by 12% and the average price of its imports fell by 2%. The terms of trade index was 100 at the start of the year. Calculate the terms of trade index at the end of the year.

Over a year, the average price of Loristan’s exports rose by 5% and the average price of its imports rose by 4%. The terms of trade index was 100 at the start of the year. Calculate the terms of trade index at the end of the year.

Extract: Zentara and Rovania are negotiating a free trade agreement. One worker in Zentara can produce 12 tonnes of fish or 6 bicycles a week; one worker in Rovania can produce 3 tonnes of fish or 12 bicycles. Over the last five years Zentara’s export price index has moved to 110 and its import price index to 100 (base year = 100). Trade unions in Zentara fear job losses in its bicycles industry, while business groups argue that tariff-free access to a larger market will bring economies of scale. Both countries are members of the WTO. (a) Using opportunity costs, explain which country has a comparative advantage in fish. (b) Calculate Zentara’s terms of trade index and state whether it has improved since the base year. (c) Explain the difference between a free trade area and a customs union.
items.answer: (a) Zentara, because it has the lower opportunity cost of fish (Zentara: 0.5, Rovania: 4 bicycles per unit). (b) 110/100 × 100 = 110; improved (favourable). (c) An FTA removes internal tariffs only; a customs union also has a common external tariff.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Zentara, because it has the lower opportunity cost of fish (Zentara: 0.5, Rovania: 4 bicycles per unit). [2] (b) Credit: 110/100 × 100 = 110; improved (favourable). [2] (c) Credit: An FTA removes internal tariffs only; a customs union also has a common external tariff. [2]

items.stem: Explain why joining a trading bloc may reduce a country’s economic welfare.
items.answer: If trade diversion outweighs trade creation, consumers pay more for imports from higher-cost members, and the government loses tariff revenue; members may also lose policy independence.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: trade diversion; 1 mark: higher cost/loss of revenue or sovereignty [2]

items.stem: A student, Freya, claims: ‘Members of a free trade area all charge the same tariff on imports from outside the area.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: That is a customs union; FTA members keep their own external tariffs, which is why rules of origin are needed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – That is a customs union; FTA members keep their own external tariffs, which is why rules of origin are needed. [2]

items.stem: Members have free internal trade and factor movement, a single currency and harmonised economic policies. What type of trading bloc is described?
options: Common market
Economic union
World Trade Organization
Free trade area
items.answer: Economic union
items.markingKey: Economic union: common market plus common currency/monetary and coordinated fiscal policy.

items.stem: Esteria has recently signed several trade agreements with its neighbours. Explain the role of the WTO in promoting international trade.
items.answer: Negotiating rounds to cut tariffs; non-discrimination (MFN, national treatment); dispute settlement; monitoring; special treatment for developing countries.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Negotiating rounds to cut tariffs; non-discrimination (MFN, national treatment); dispute settlement; monitoring; special treatment for developing countries. Level 3 (6–8): accurate knowledge with a clear, developed analytical chain and, where relevant, an accurate, labelled diagram that is used in the answer; Level 2 (3–5): some correct explanation but undeveloped or partly inaccurate; Level 1 (1–2): limited knowledge, mostly assertion [8]

items.stem: Country X can produce 10 units of food or 5 units of clothing with one worker. What is the opportunity cost of 1 unit of clothing in Country X?
options: 2 units of food
10 units of food
0.5 units of food
5 units of food
items.answer: 2 units of food
items.markingKey: 10 food / 5 clothing = 2 units of food per unit of clothing.

items.stem: Explain why comparative advantage can change over time.
items.answer: Opportunity costs depend on factor endowments, skills, technology and investment, which change; e.g. education and FDI can give a country a new comparative advantage in manufactured goods or services.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: depends on factor endowments/technology; 1 mark: example of change [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain the difference between absolute advantage and comparative advantage. (b) Explain why comparative advantage can change over time.
items.answer: (a) Absolute advantage means producing more of a good than another country with the same resources. Comparative advantage means producing a good at a lower opportunity cost, i.e. giving up less of the other good. (b) Opportunity costs depend on factor endowments, skills, technology and investment, which change; e.g. education and FDI can give a country a new comparative advantage in manufactured goods or services.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: absolute = more output from same resources; 1 mark: comparative = lower opportunity cost [2] (b) 1 mark: depends on factor endowments/technology; 1 mark: example of change [2]

items.stem: Kestria has invested heavily in education and now exports software services. What is the most likely source of this country’s comparative advantage?
options: Comparative advantage based on human capital
Comparative advantage based on labour abundance
Comparative advantage based on capital and technology
Comparative advantage based on natural resources
items.answer: Comparative advantage based on human capital
items.markingKey: Comparative advantage based on human capital: skilled labour lowers the opportunity cost of skill-intensive services.

items.stem: One worker in Sundara can produce either 6 bags of coffee or 4 machine tools a week. One worker in Umbria Nova can produce either 4 bags of coffee or 8 machine tools a week. On the basis of comparative advantage, which pattern of specialisation would increase total output?
options: Each country should produce both goods equally
Umbria Nova should specialise in coffee and Sundara in machine tools
Sundara should specialise in coffee and Umbria Nova in machine tools
Neither country can gain from specialisation
items.answer: Sundara should specialise in coffee and Umbria Nova in machine tools
items.markingKey: OC of 1 unit of coffee: Sundara 0.67, Umbria Nova 2 machine tools; Sundara has the lower OC of coffee.

items.stem: Extract: Tarvia and Rovania are negotiating a free trade agreement. One worker in Tarvia can produce 8 tonnes of fish or 12 bicycles a week; one worker in Rovania can produce 4 tonnes of fish or 4 bicycles. Over the last five years Tarvia’s export price index has moved to 92 and its import price index to 94 (base year = 100). Trade unions in Tarvia fear job losses in its fish industry, while business groups argue that tariff-free access to a larger market will bring economies of scale. Both countries are members of the WTO. (a) Calculate Tarvia’s terms of trade index and state whether it has improved since the base year. (b) Discuss whether Tarvia should sign the free trade agreement.
items.answer: (a) 92/94 × 100 = 97.9; worsened (unfavourable). (b) Gains: specialisation, lower prices, economies of scale, competition, FDI. Costs: structural unemployment, adjustment costs, over-specialisation, possible trade diversion; depends on size of gains, mobility of labour and support for displaced workers; judgement.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: 92/94 × 100 = 97.9; worsened (unfavourable). [2] (b) Credit: Gains: specialisation, lower prices, economies of scale, competition, FDI. Costs: structural unemployment, adjustment costs, over-specialisation, possible trade diversion; depends on size of gains, mobility of labour and support for displaced workers; judgement. [6]

items.stem: How can free trade allow firms to benefit from economies of scale?
options: It raises the prices of imports
It gives them access to larger world markets
It reduces the size of their market
It protects them from foreign competition
items.answer: It gives them access to larger world markets
items.markingKey: Larger output lowers average cost.

items.stem: Jonas makes the following statement: ‘Free trade benefits every worker in Dravonia.’ Identify the error in this statement and correct it.
items.answer: Free trade raises total welfare, but workers in import-competing industries may lose jobs; there are winners and losers.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Free trade raises total welfare, but workers in import-competing industries may lose jobs; there are winners and losers. [2]

items.stem: Umbria Nova and Istrana each have 100 workers. One worker in Umbria Nova can produce 12 tonnes of wheat or 10 cars; one worker in Istrana can produce 10 tonnes of wheat or 4 cars. Before trade, each country uses half its workers in each industry. What is the combined output of the two countries before trade?
options: 1100 tonnes of wheat and 700 cars
550 tonnes of wheat and 350 cars
1000 tonnes of wheat and 1000 cars
2200 tonnes of wheat and 1400 cars
items.answer: 1100 tonnes of wheat and 700 cars

items.stem: Domestic paper producers in Zentara close factories after cheaper imports arrive. Which effect of free trade and specialisation does this illustrate? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Cost of free trade: structural unemployment: workers in import-competing industries lose jobs and may lack transferable skills.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Cost of free trade: structural unemployment; 1 mark: explanation – workers in import-competing industries lose jobs and may lack transferable skills. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Valdoria and Quentara are negotiating a free trade agreement. One worker in Valdoria can produce 5 bags of coffee or 6 machine tools a week; one worker in Quentara can produce 12 bags of coffee or 4 machine tools. Over the last five years Valdoria’s export price index has moved to 92 and its import price index to 94 (base year = 100). Trade unions in Valdoria fear job losses in its coffee industry, while business groups argue that tariff-free access to a larger market will bring economies of scale. Both countries are members of the WTO. (a) Calculate Valdoria’s terms of trade index and state whether it has improved since the base year. (b) Explain why trade unions fear job losses.
items.answer: (a) 92/94 × 100 = 97.9; worsened (unfavourable). (b) Resources move out of the industry with comparative disadvantage; cheaper imports replace domestic output; workers may be occupationally immobile.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: 92/94 × 100 = 97.9; worsened (unfavourable). [2] (b) Credit: Resources move out of the industry with comparative disadvantage; cheaper imports replace domestic output; workers may be occupationally immobile. [3]

items.stem: Which would cause a country’s terms of trade to deteriorate?
options: A fall in the prices of its imports
An appreciation of its currency
A fall in world prices of its main exports
A rise in world prices of its main exports
items.answer: A fall in world prices of its main exports
items.markingKey: Export price index falls relative to import index.

items.stem: In a revision note Noah wrote: ‘The terms of trade measure the quantity of exports compared with the quantity of imports.’ Identify what is wrong with this reasoning and give the correct explanation.
items.answer: The terms of trade compare average export prices with average import prices, not quantities.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – The terms of trade compare average export prices with average import prices, not quantities. [2]

items.stem: Inflation in Valdoria is 9% while inflation in its trading partners is 2%. What is the likely effect on the terms of trade of Valdoria?
options: Deterioration in the terms of trade
Improvement in the terms of trade
An increase in export volumes only
No change in the terms of trade
items.answer: Improvement in the terms of trade
items.markingKey: Improvement in the terms of trade: domestic export prices rise faster than import prices.

items.stem: A bumper harvest across producing countries lowers the world price of coffee, Quentara’s main export. What is the likely effect on the terms of trade of Quentara? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Deterioration in the terms of trade: export prices fall relative to import prices.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Deterioration in the terms of trade; 1 mark: explanation – export prices fall relative to import prices. [2]

items.stem: Extract: Quentara and Esteria are negotiating a free trade agreement. One worker in Quentara can produce 6 bags of coffee or 2 machine tools a week; one worker in Esteria can produce 5 bags of coffee or 12 machine tools. Over the last five years Quentara’s export price index has moved to 96 and its import price index to 94 (base year = 100). Trade unions in Quentara fear job losses in its machine tools industry, while business groups argue that tariff-free access to a larger market will bring economies of scale. Both countries are members of the WTO. (a) Calculate the opportunity cost of 1 unit of coffee in each country. (b) Using opportunity costs, explain which country has a comparative advantage in coffee. (c) Explain the difference between a free trade area and a customs union.
items.answer: (a) Quentara: 0.33 machine tools; Esteria: 2.4 machine tools. (b) Quentara, because it has the lower opportunity cost of coffee (Quentara: 0.33, Esteria: 2.4 machine tools per unit). (c) An FTA removes internal tariffs only; a customs union also has a common external tariff.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Quentara: 0.33 machine tools; Esteria: 2.4 machine tools. [2] (b) Credit: Quentara, because it has the lower opportunity cost of coffee (Quentara: 0.33, Esteria: 2.4 machine tools per unit). [2] (c) Credit: An FTA removes internal tariffs only; a customs union also has a common external tariff. [2]

items.stem: Sipho wrote in a homework answer: ‘The WTO sets the tariffs that each country must charge.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: The WTO provides rules and a forum for negotiating tariff reductions and settling disputes; members agree their own maximum (bound) tariffs.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – The WTO provides rules and a forum for negotiating tariff reductions and settling disputes; members agree their own maximum (bound) tariffs. [2]

items.stem: During a class discussion Isla said: ‘Joining a customs union always increases efficiency because tariffs are removed.’ Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Removing internal tariffs can cause trade creation, but the common external tariff can cause trade diversion to higher-cost members, reducing efficiency.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error; 1 mark: correct explanation – Removing internal tariffs can cause trade creation, but the common external tariff can cause trade diversion to higher-cost members, reducing efficiency. [2]

items.stem: Tarvia imports chocolate bars. Before joining a customs union, Tarvia charged a 20% tariff on all imports. Marvona (outside the union) supplies chocolate bars at $40 per unit and Ostrelia (a union partner) at $46 per unit. After joining, imports from Ostrelia are tariff-free, while the common external tariff on Marvona stays at 20%. After Tarvia joins, what is the price of chocolate bars imported from Marvona?

Extract: Halvoria and Jovania are negotiating a free trade agreement. One worker in Halvoria can produce 2 tonnes of fish or 10 bicycles a week; one worker in Jovania can produce 5 tonnes of fish or 2 bicycles. Over the last five years Halvoria’s export price index has moved to 96 and its import price index to 94 (base year = 100). Trade unions in Halvoria fear job losses in its fish industry, while business groups argue that tariff-free access to a larger market will bring economies of scale. Both countries are members of the WTO. (a) Using opportunity costs, explain which country has a comparative advantage in fish. (b) Discuss whether Halvoria should sign the free trade agreement.
items.answer: (a) Jovania, because it has the lower opportunity cost of fish (Halvoria: 5, Jovania: 0.4 bicycles per unit). (b) Gains: specialisation, lower prices, economies of scale, competition, FDI. Costs: structural unemployment, adjustment costs, over-specialisation, possible trade diversion; depends on size of gains, mobility of labour and support for displaced workers; judgement.
